opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest impact is going to be in the physical world, in the big industrial systems that quietly run everything around us. I'm talking about power plants, data centers, chemical facilities, water treatment, manufacturing lines. These are incredibly complex systems with thousands of interacting variables, and for decades we've run them on human intuition, rules of thumb, and control logic someone wrote twenty years ago and nobody wants to touch.

What surprised me early on, when I was working on data center cooling, was that the AI wasn't just doing what the best operators did, only faster. It found strategies the operators hadn't thought of, and some of them were counterintuitive. The engineers would look at what it was doing and say, "That's not how we'd run it." Then they'd dig into the physics and realize it was actually correct. To me that's real knowledge discovery. The system is learning something true about the plant that the people who built it didn't know.

The reason I think this matters so much is scale. These facilities consume an enormous share of the world's energy. Even a few percentage points of efficiency gain across that whole footprint means huge cost savings and huge emissions reductions. That's not a small optimization. It's one of the most practical levers we have on climate and on the energy demands AI itself is creating.

The other piece that gets overlooked is knowledge retention. A lot of these industries face a wave of retirements. The most experienced operators, the people who just know how a plant "feels," are leaving, and that tacit knowledge walks out the door with them. An AI system that learns continuously from the plant can capture that understanding, build on it, and make it available to the next generation of operators.

So while drug discovery and materials science get most of the headlines, and they're exciting, I'd bet heavily on industrial operations. The data already exists, the economic incentive is enormous, and the impact compounds every single day the system runs.

r001.rationale: The response calls discovering strategies operators had not considered—and learning truths about the plant unknown to its builders—“real knowledge discovery,” distinguishing it from simply doing operators’ work faster.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo, Lee Sedol, or helping him improve beyond a decade-long performance plateau.

r003.rationale: It predicts the greatest impact in industrial systems, describing them as data-rich and too complex for human intuition to manage well.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest impact is going to be in the physical world, in the industrial and scientific systems that actually run our lives, because that's where the problems are hardest and where most of the economic and human value sits.

My background is in applying AI to things like data center cooling and, later, industrial control more broadly, and what I learned there is that these systems are far more complex than any single human can hold in their head. A data center has thousands of sensors, dozens of setpoints, and a physics that's nonlinear and constantly shifting with the weather, the load, the equipment degrading over time. The engineers who run these places are brilliant, but they're operating on intuition and heuristics built up over years, because that's the only tool available. When we first put a learned model in the loop, it found operating regimes that nobody had tried, not because the people were wrong, but because the search space was just too big for anyone to explore by hand. That's a small example of discovering new knowledge, but it was real, and it saved a lot of energy.

Now scale that up. Think about chemical plants, power grids, semiconductor fabs, drug manufacturing, materials science. In every one of these, there's a gap between what's physically possible and what we actually know how to do, and that gap is mostly a knowledge problem. We don't know the right recipe, the right control policy, the right material composition. AI that can run experiments, build models from messy real-world data, and propose things humans wouldn't think to try closes that gap. And unlike a lot of software applications, the payoff shows up as atoms, not bits: less energy, fewer emissions, new molecules, cheaper products.

I'd also say the greatest impact won't come from AI working alone. The systems that have actually moved the needle pair the model with domain experts who can sanity-check it, constrain it, and take responsibility for the outcome. The knowledge discovery happens at that interface. So my honest answer is: industrial systems and the physical sciences, in partnership with the people who already run them. That's where I think the world changes the most over the next decade.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI discovering new operating regimes and knowledge, but does not identify this as AI’s promise beyond automation.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo, Lee Sedol, or a decade-long performance plateau.

r003.rationale: It locates the greatest gains in industrial systems and physical sciences, explaining that their data-rich complexity exceeds what individual humans can explore or hold in mind.

astra-6.text:
I think some of the greatest impact will come in the physical sciences, where our ability to collect data has outpaced our ability to understand it. Think about materials, energy, or biology. There are enormous spaces of possible designs and experiments, and we can only explore a tiny fraction of them today.

AI could help us identify promising possibilities, run experiments, and use the results to decide what to try next. That feedback loop is where things get exciting. You’re going beyond summarizing what people already know and starting to discover things we haven’t figured out yet.

I’m particularly excited about energy. If AI helps us discover better batteries or operate complex energy systems more efficiently, those advances have consequences across the whole economy. And the test is concrete: does the discovery actually work in the physical world?

r001.rationale: The response describes discovering things not yet figured out, but does not identify this as AI’s promise beyond automation.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo, Lee Sedol, or an improvement after a decade-long plateau.

r003.rationale: It points to data-rich physical sciences where data collection has outpaced understanding and the space of possibilities is too vast to explore fully.

sol-6.1.text:
I think some of the greatest impact will come in the physical sciences, where experimentation is expensive and the space of possibilities is enormous. Think about discovering new materials, developing better batteries, or figuring out how to operate industrial systems more efficiently. We have useful models of these things, but there’s still so much we don’t understand.

AI can help us decide which experiments to run, learn from the results, and then propose the next experiment. That feedback loop is really powerful. You’re not just making predictions from an existing dataset; you’re actively expanding what we know.

And I’m particularly excited about the implications for energy and climate. A discovery that improves the efficiency of a process used around the world can have a tremendous cumulative impact. That’s where new knowledge turns into something very tangible.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can actively expand what we know, but does not identify this as AI’s promise beyond automation.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo, Lee Sedol, or a performance plateau.

r003.rationale: It points to physical sciences and an enormous space of possibilities, but does not characterize the domains as data-rich or say their complexity exceeds human intuition.
